repaired_payload.caption:
Think 'No-Cost EMI' means zero interest costs? Here is how a Rs 164900 iPhone 18 Pro purchase actually gets billed during festive sales.

• Buyer A pays Rs 164900 upfront.
• Buyer B pays standard credit card interest on top.
• Buyer C takes 'no-cost' EMI—where seller discounts the interest, but GST on bank interest remains payable.

Save this breakdown before shopping the next festive sale.

When buying big-ticket items, do you prefer paying full upfront or absorbing the hidden GST fee across EMIs?

slides.title: Three buyers, one Rs 164900 phone: Who really saved the most?

slides.headline: The Three Festive Shoppers
slides.card_text:
Buyer A paid Rs 164900 full upfront for iPhone 18 Pro.
Buyer B picked standard credit card EMI.
Buyer C chose festive no-cost EMI.

slides.headline: The Common Assumption About No-Cost EMI

comparison_data.myth: No-cost EMI means the bank does not charge any interest.
comparison_data.reality: The bank still charges interest; the seller readjusts the amount upfront so EMIs total the original price.

slides.headline: How the Math Is Rearranged
flowchart_data: 1. Seller readjusts interest to match total upfront tag
2. Bank converts balance into an interest-bearing EMI loan
3. Sum of all EMIs equals the original retail price
slides.highlighted_phrase: Sum of all EMIs equals the original retail price

slides.headline: The Hidden Catch: Tax on Interest
slides.card_text: Even though the seller readjusts the interest amount, interest still exists. Bank interest legally attracts GST, which is billed directly to Buyer C.

checklist_data.text: Buyer B: Paid retail tag + interest + GST
Buyer C: Paid retail tag + GST on bank interest
Buyer A: Paid exactly Rs 164900 upfront with zero extra tax on interest
